Recap / current assumptions from Nimbus:
- Peak concurrent active requests: ~250 (short spikes up to 320 during batch ingest windows)
- Sustained concurrent: ~110-130 during business hours
- Streaming websocket connections: ~40 concurrently (we stream partial outputs for live clinical notes)
- Typical request size: 512 tokens input, 256 tokens output (mostly short summaries)
- Latency requirement: p95 end-to-end < 200ms for 90% of requests; for streaming we need first token < 120ms and steady chunk latency < 100ms

Attachments: I included a short perf snippet from our canary (Nimbus_perf_report.log).

Questions:
1) How should we think about concurrency quotas vs. per-minute rate limits for this workload?
2) Do you recommend connection pooling or per-request connections for best latency with streaming?
3) If we go Dedicated, what buffer/burst headroom would Redwood recommend to handle spikes (e.g., 320->400)?

Alex - thanks for the clear recap. Great to see the perf snippet; that helps a lot. Below is a concise response and a recommended next step (technical deep-dive + draft capacity plan).

Short answers (high-level):
- Quotas vs rate limits: we operate two levers - concurrent request quota (how many parallel requests your account can have against a given model/route) and sustained rate quotas (requests/min or tokens/min). For low-latency streaming workloads the concurrency quota is the dominant control.
- Connection pooling: we strongly recommend persistent connections (HTTP/2 or websockets) with keep-alive for streaming - fewer connection handshakes means lower tail latency and more efficient multiplexing. Our SDKs default to connection reuse and recommend a client-side pool of ~16-32 connections per host depending on thread models.
- Burst headroom: for Dedicated customers we typically size committed concurrency at ~1.25x your sustained peak and offer burst capacity (on-demand) up to 1.5-1.8x depending on instance availability. For Nimbus numbers that suggests committed concurrency ~160, reserved burst to ~400 for short periods.

Redwood preliminary proposal (attached PDF):
- Committed concurrency: 160 dedicated slots
- Sustained RPS quota: 2,000 requests/min (based on your request mix)
- Burst capacity: up to 400 concurrent requests for 10-minute windows
- Streaming connections: 50 concurrent websockets (to cover 40 active + headroom)
- Rate limiting behavior: soft throttles at sustained quota; hard throttles once burst budget exhausted; 429 responses include X-Redwood-Quota and Retry-After headers.

Telemetry we need for final quote: distribution of request inter-arrival (per-minute), percent of requests that use streaming vs unary, and any scheduled batch windows when spikes occur. The SLO_checklist.xlsx I attached shows the exact fields we use.

Proposed next step: schedule a 60-minute technical deep-dive with Laura (solutions engineer) and your engineering lead to walk through connection pooling, KV-cache patterns, and a quick canary plan. Ben is on copy for commercial sizing/contract.

I can do Wed 9/15 10-11am PT or Thu 9/16 8-11am PT - what works?

Thanks,

- Marissa

Marissa/Alex - quick clarifications from our side before the deep-dive:
- Connection pooling: when you say "client-side pool of ~16-32 connections per host", is that per app server instance or total per region? Our frontend fleet has ~60 instances that could each open up to 8 streams. We want to avoid accidental over-saturation.
- Streaming semantics: How does Redwood surface partial tokens for backpressure? Do we get chunked events with sequence IDs? Any guidance on max chunk size to avoid head-of-line blocking?
- 429 behavior: If we hit a soft throttle, can Redwood queue or does it immediately return 429? We prefer graceful queuing for short bursts instead of errors.

Also - one of our compliance folks asked if you can share typical observability fields (trace IDs, per-token cost breakdown, socket-level metrics) so we can map to our dashboards.

- Priya
Senior Platform Engineer, Nimbus Health

Priya - great questions. Short answers here; we'll cover details in the deep-dive and I'll attach a short tech note in the calendar invite.

- Pooling guidance: the 16-32 connections guidance is per app-server *instance* when you are multiplexing many logical streams over HTTP/2. If each instance opens 8 streams you'll want fewer connections (e.g., 8-12) because multiplexing will cover them. We'll work with your infra team to map expected total concurrent streams (instances x streams) to a safe account-level concurrency target.
- Streaming events & backpressure: Redwood streams partial tokens as chunked frames over HTTP/2 or websocket messages with sequence metadata. We recommend small-ish chunk sizes (e.g., 64-128 tokens per chunk) to reduce head-of-line blocking for interleaved streams. The SDK surfaces a Rechunker utility for steady chunk emission.
- 429 / soft throttle behavior: for Hosted customers we offer "grace window" queuing up to the burst budget (short windows, typically <= 2 minutes); when the grace window is full we return 429 with Retry-After. For Dedicated customers we can enable a configurable queuing policy (drop-oldest or allow short latency tail growth) - we'll capture your preference in the MUTUAL ACTION PLAN.

Observability: we include trace IDs in X-Redwood-Trace and per-request token/cost breakdown in response headers for every completed request. Socket-level metrics and per-connection stats are available in the Console (we can add a sample dashboard link).

Next steps I actioned:
- Sending calendar invite for deep-dive w/Laura & Ben (attach tech note + Redwood_concurrency_proposal.pdf).
- Ben will follow up with a draft commercial term sheet (committed concurrency, burst pricing).

If you can share your per-minute arrival distribution and confirm whether batch windows are scheduled (time-of-day), we can finalize recommended committed capacity before the call.

Thanks - look forward to the deep-dive.
